title: Composition and affine examples of quasi-compact quasi-separated stack morphisms
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $\mathcal X\xrightarrow{f}\mathcal Y\xrightarrow{g}\mathcal Z$ be morphisms of algebraic stacks over $k$ [def-sfb-algebraic-moduli-stack]. Use quasi-compact and quasi-separated morphisms as in [def-sfb-stack-qcqs-morphism]. If $f$ and $g$ are quasi-compact and quasi-separated, then $g\circ f$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated. An affine morphism $q:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ of algebraic stacks over $k$ is quasi-compact and quasi-separated; here affine means that for every scheme $T\to\mathcal B$, the $2$-fibre product $\mathcal A\times_{\mathcal B}T$ is a scheme and its projection to $T$ has affine inverse images of affine open subsets [def-pc-scheme]. No finite-type, Noetherian or condition on the absolute diagonals is imposed.

source.place: Tags 050W (lemma-composition-quasi-compact), 050K (lemma-composition-separated), quasi-separated clause; 050T (lemma-characterize-representable-quasi-compact), 04YT (lemma-representable-quasi-separated-diagonal-quasi-compact); 0CHQ (definition-affine) and 01S7 (lemma-affine-separated). Affine scheme inverse images are quasi-compact by their definition.

proof.text: Let $\mathcal T\to\mathcal Z$ be a quasi-compact algebraic-stack test. The stack $\mathcal D=\mathcal Y\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal T$ is quasi-compact by the definition for $g$, and $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal D$ is quasi-compact by the definition for $f$. These are algebraic stacks by the fibre-product lemma. The triples defining the products give an equivalence $\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal D\simeq\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal T$: send $(x,(y,t,\beta),\alpha:f(x)\simeq y)$ to $(x,t,\beta\circ g(\alpha))$, with inverse $(x,t,\gamma)\mapsto(x,(f(x),t,\gamma),\mathrm{id})$. These functors are inverse up to the isomorphism supplied by $\alpha$. Transporting a smooth surjective atlas along this equivalence retains its quasi-compact scheme source, so $gf$ is quasi-compact. This argument uses only quasi-compactness of $f,g$.

For the diagonal calculation, consider a morphism $p:\mathcal U\to\mathcal V$ of algebraic stacks, representable by algebraic spaces, all of whose scheme tests are quasi-compact and quasi-separated algebraic-space maps. Any base change of $p$ along a morphism of algebraic stacks is a morphism of algebraic stacks by the fibre-product lemma, and is representable by the representability calculus. Each scheme test of the base change is, by associativity of triples, a scheme test of $p$ itself; hence it again has both properties. For composition, let $r:\mathcal V\to\mathcal W$ be another such representable morphism of algebraic stacks. The scheme-test equivalence makes $p$ and $r$ quasi-compact stack maps. The argument of step 1 makes $rp$ quasi-compact. Representability of $rp$ and the converse scheme-test equivalence imply that every scheme test of $rp$ is quasi-compact as a space morphism.

proof.text: Keep $p,r$ as in step 2. For a scheme $T\to\mathcal W$ put $V_T=\mathcal V\times_{\mathcal W}T$. This is an algebraic space, and $r_T:V_T\to T$ is quasi-separated by assumption. The pullback $U_T=\mathcal U\times_{\mathcal V}V_T$ is an algebraic space by the space-valued representable-pullback lemma. Every scheme base change of $p_{V_T}:U_T\to V_T$ is a scheme test of $p$, by associativity of the displayed triples, and is therefore quasi-separated. The new space scheme-test criterion makes $p_{V_T}$ quasi-separated. Its composition with $r_T$ is quasi-separated by the space composition clause, and is exactly the scheme test of $rp$. Thus every scheme test of $rp$ has both required properties, the quasi-compact part having been proved in step 2.

The definition of quasi-separatedness says that $\Delta_f$ and $\Delta_g$ are representable and all their scheme tests are quasi-compact and quasi-separated. Put $P=\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Y}\mathcal X$ and $Q=\mathcal X\times_{\mathcal Z}\mathcal X$. These are algebraic stacks by the fibre-product lemma, so steps 2 and 3 apply to maps between $\mathcal X$, $P$ and $Q$. Identity (2) of the diagonal-pullback node, applied with $u=v=f$ and $h=g$, identifies $i:P\to Q$ as the base change of $\Delta_g$. Step 2 gives the required properties for $i$. The factorization $\mathcal X\xrightarrow{\Delta_f}P\xrightarrow{i}Q$ sends $x$ to $(x,x,\mathrm{id}_{gf(x)})$, hence is $\Delta_{gf}$. Steps 2 and 3 give its representability and quasi-compact quasi-separated scheme tests. Thus $gf$ is quasi-separated, completing the composition clause.

Let $q:\mathcal A\to\mathcal B$ be affine. Every scheme test $a_T:A_T\to T$ is an affine scheme morphism. For any quasi-compact algebraic space $C\to T$, choose a surjective etale scheme atlas $U\to C$ with $U$ quasi-compact. The base change $A_U\to U$ is affine, hence quasi-compact as a scheme morphism by affine permanence. The inverse-image lemma, with the quasi-compact open $W=U$, makes $A_U$ quasi-compact. Base change of the atlas gives a representable surjective etale map $A_U\to A_T\times_TC$ by the space fibre-product lemma. It is therefore a quasi-compact scheme atlas of this product. This proves intrinsic algebraic-space quasi-compactness of $a_T$, including tests by nonschematic $C$. The affine-locality node makes $a_T$ separated: its further affine scheme tests have affine scheme source by affine base change, exactly that node's affine hypothesis. The separated-implies-quasi-separated clause of the new node now gives intrinsic quasi-separatedness. The representable scheme-test equivalence makes $q$ a quasi-compact stack morphism. We will also use the properties of $a_T$ just proved for any affine scheme morphism, including a closed immersion, which is affine by its affine-local definition.

Fix a scheme test $T\to\mathcal A\times_{\mathcal B}\mathcal A$, given by $(x_1,x_2,\alpha:q(x_1)\simeq q(x_2))$. Let $A_T=\mathcal A\times_{\mathcal B}T$ using the map $q(x_1):T\to\mathcal B$. It is a scheme affine over $T$. The objects $(x_1,\mathrm{id})$ and $(x_2,\alpha^{-1})$ are sections $s_1,s_2:T\to A_T$. The test of $\Delta_q$ is their equality locus $T\times_{A_T\times_T A_T}A_T$. Indeed a lift of the stack diagonal is an isomorphism $\beta:x_1\simeq x_2$ satisfying $q(\beta)=\alpha$; this is exactly the arrow condition between those sections in the discrete algebraic space $A_T$. Sending a diagonal lift with its two identifications to their composite gives this bijection, with inverse the lift $x_1$ and the identifications $\mathrm{id},\beta$; these constructions commute with pullback. This is the diagonal base-change identification of the cited node. The affine scheme map $A_T\to T$ is separated, so its diagonal is a closed immersion. Base change gives that the displayed equality locus is a scheme closed-immersed in $T$. It is affine by the closed-immersion definition, and step 5 gives intrinsic space quasi-compactness and quasi-separatedness of this test. Every scheme test of $\Delta_q$ is therefore a space with both properties. This is exactly quasi-separatedness of $q$ in the given definition; together with step 5 it proves the affine clause.
